# Five-minute website walkthrough

English synthetic narration (macOS Samantha). Actual website states captured from the project.

## 00:00:00 — 01 / The decision and intended user

Cambridge Storefront Opportunity helps city staff and prospective business owners screen business categories and storefront locations before investing. It combines observed vacancies and regional business supply with an editable price and cost scenario to select ideas worth testing. The website separates measured evidence from hypothetical inputs, and does not claim that an empty storefront proves unmet customer demand.

## 00:00:25 — 02 / Read the decision brief

The dashboard uses the September twenty twenty-five storefront snapshot, not a live inventory of spaces available today. The district chart compares counts and estimated average vacancy months, while the profile chart groups spaces by duration and size. Boston food-license additions provide separate regional context; they are not a direct measure of Cambridge competition or customer demand.

## 00:00:50 — 03 / Trace the data and protect privacy

The Method page explains public data from Cambridge, Boston, the Census Bureau, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Cambridge and Boston were re-fetched on September twenty-second with server-side field selection, excluding names, contacts, home locations and permit identifiers from requests. The pipeline checks returned fields and row counts and stops on unexpected fields, without falling back to a complete source file.

## 00:01:15 — 04 / Understand the measures

Cambridge reports a vacancy year rather than an exact date, so July is assumed when estimating vacancy duration. The priority score multiplies the number of reported storefronts by their estimated average vacancy months within each district. This combines vacancy volume with persistence, but it is an outreach ranking, not a forecast of profitability or investment returns.

## 00:01:40 — 05 / Start an interactive comparison

On Explore, the initial view includes all commercial districts in the latest snapshot, with ninety-six reported storefront records. The left panel controls district selection, reported floor area, and minimum estimated vacancy duration; the chart responds to these selections. The Boston year controls affect the separate license context, so the two record counts should not be confused or combined.

## 00:02:05 — 06 / Change the district selection

Here, East Cambridge is unchecked to demonstrate how a district selection changes the records included in the comparison. The storefront count and chart update together, allowing an analyst to focus the discussion on the remaining commercial districts. The selected filters also appear in the page address, making a particular comparison shareable with colleagues preparing the same briefing.

## 00:02:30 — 07 / Compare districts with the same filters

Next, the Districts control switches the same filtered records into a district comparison without resetting the selection. Bar length shows the number of storefront records, while color encodes estimated average duration, giving two views of vacancy pressure. A district with many recent vacancies may need a different response from one with fewer spaces that have remained empty longer.

## 00:02:55 — 08 / Investigate persistent vacancies

The minimum estimated vacancy is now set to thirty-six months, and the Vacancy profile view groups the remaining spaces. This interaction narrows the question from all reported vacancies to spaces estimated to have been empty for at least three years. The size bands help shape a targeted support proposal, but missing floor area and approximate dates still require case-by-case follow-up.

## 00:03:20 — 09 / Compare business-category hypotheses

The market opportunity section compares retail, food services, and personal services using Census employer establishments and employment for the selected county. Middlesex includes Cambridge, but these are regional supply statistics, not a list of local competitors or evidence of a market gap. Choose a category to see a concrete pilot concept and the missing price, preference and repeat-purchase evidence needed to validate it.

## 00:03:45 — 10 / Test price and sales assumptions

The calculator starts with hypothetical prices and costs, requiring twenty-six daily sales under the displayed default assumptions. Here the sale price changes from fifteen to twenty dollars, holding other costs constant; the calculated requirement falls to seventeen sales per day. This is a break-even condition, not a demand forecast: customers might buy less at a higher price, so a paid pilot remains essential.

## 00:04:10 — 11 / Turn findings into practical actions

First, prioritize an initial outreach cycle in Central and Harvard Squares, then review progress after ninety days. Second, pilot small-space assistance for the thirteen observed spaces below fifteen hundred square feet estimated vacant for more than a year. Third, offer an opt-in pathway for permitted cottage-food operators to explore shared kitchens or storefront testing, without assuming that every operator wants expansion.

## 00:04:35 — 12 / Explain the limits and next evidence

These administrative records support prioritizing investigation, but cannot explain why a space is empty or prove that public support causes occupancy. Year-only dates create uncertainty of roughly six months, and reported inventories can miss spaces or reflect changing collection practices. Before funding decisions, add rents, lease terms, foot traffic, accessibility, and voluntary stakeholder feedback; use this website as a starting point for that investigation.
